detail:
The Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH) reports that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration qualified a change in total-hip bone mineral density (BMD), measured by DXA, as a surrogate endpoint for use in osteoporosis clinical trials. The qualification grew out of the SABRE project, a public-private partnership that pooled data from many trials to show that treatment-related changes in total-hip BMD reliably predict reductions in fracture risk. A surrogate endpoint is a measured substitute used in trials in place of a direct clinical outcome such as fracture.

FNIH presents the qualification explicitly as a clinical trial methods advance, not as a new treatment and not as a new screening rule for individual patients. According to the announcement, having a qualified surrogate endpoint is expected to make future osteoporosis trials smaller, shorter, and more feasible, which may speed the development and evaluation of new therapies. The announcement does not change how clinicians diagnose osteoporosis or decide treatment for an individual, which sources continue to base on bone density, fracture history, and overall risk assessment.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about osteoporosis clinical trial research.
sourceName: Foundation for the National Institutes of Health
summary: FNIH reports FDA qualification of total-hip BMD change as the first surrogate endpoint for osteoporosis trials under the SABRE project, a trial-methods advance that is not a new treatment or screening rule.
takeaways: total-hip BMD change was qualified as a surrogate endpoint for trials
the SABRE project pooled trial data linking BMD change to fracture risk
sources frame the step as trial methods, not a treatment or screening change
title: Osteoporosis: a qualified surrogate endpoint to speed clinical trials
